Yes, the story has an appropriate balance between scene and summary/exposition. 

The vast majority of the story unfolds in vivid, real-time scenes—from the initial encounter by the burned chair, to the narrator following the couple through the rising floodwaters, to the tense observation outside their window. These dramatized moments effectively build atmosphere and suspense through specific actions, visual details, and brief dialogue. 

The writer seamlessly weaves in a small, necessary amount of exposition—specifically, the two brief paragraphs explaining the narrator's eleven-year history of preparing apartment inventories and his recently lost job. Rather than bogging the story down, this concise summary provides the exact context needed to understand the narrator's obsessive attention to detail and why he feels compelled to follow the couple, thereby enriching the real-time scenes that make up the rest of the narrative.
